name: Priya Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for Highland Rural Electric, a small co-op owned by the people it supplies, mostly farms and hill villages. There are forty of us in total and our crew is six. I'm the junior. I dig, I flag traffic, I hand things up, I learn the knots I keep getting wrong, and on a good day Walt lets me go up in the bucket. I was a bookkeeper at a builders' merchant in Carrow for thirty years before this.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up on a line crew?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The merchant got bought by a chain, and the chain moved the accounts to a head office with some software that did my job. I was 55. My late brother worked at the co-op for twenty-five years, and Walt, the crew boss, knew me from his funeral and said they were short. I like the fresh air and the quiet roads. What wears me out is being the slowest at everything and the cold in my hands in January. I've taken over the crew's stock list, on paper, because that's the one thing I'm faster at than anybody.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. I'm going to walk you through five pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't say much. Maybe, “Well, that's that, then,” over tea. I'm not one for posting things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I finish my apprenticeship and work till 66, if my knees agree. That's eight years. With what I've got saved and the co-op pension, Ken and I would be all right, not rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep turning up, get through my climbing assessment, and keep putting a little away. I'd keep doing the stock list on paper, because nobody's asked me to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. That's how I like my days.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lost your last job partly to software. Would even small changes worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. At the merchant it started small too. First the stock went on a computer, then the invoices, then me. But a co-op this size still keeps its pole records in a filing cabinet, so I'm not losing sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your savings cushion look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About two and a half months of what we spend. Ken works three days at the garden centre, because of his hip. I keep our household books in a notebook, every coin, so I know exactly where we stand.

S0.say: She wouldn't say much publicly, perhaps a quiet “that's that, then” over tea. She doesn't post things online.
S0.think: Privately it means she finishes her apprenticeship and works to 66 if her knees allow. With modest savings and the co-op pension, she and her partner would be all right but not rich.
S0.do: Keeps turning up, gets through her climbing assessment and keeps saving a little each month. Carries on keeping the crew's stock list on paper.
S0.feel: Calm, which is how she likes her days.
S0.quote: First the stock went on a computer, then the invoices, then me.
S0.fieldNote: Priya speaks in short, exact sentences and tracks money to the coin. Her last job loss to software is never far away, but she finds comfort in how old-fashioned the small co-op is. She has carved out a niche doing the crew's stock list on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's sensible to use what works and leave the rest. Nobody would get angry with me for saying that. I'd also say the co-op shouldn't buy anything just because the big companies have it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the co-op would be last to change, which is good for me. But the stock list, the job planning and the office would probably go onto a computer first. My little paper niche would be gone, and then I'm just the slow digger again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see what the co-op actually does before I did anything. I'd save harder, maybe 50 more a month by cutting the newspaper and one of our streaming services. If they put the stock list on a computer, I'd let the young ones take it rather than learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like hearing that the chain had bought the merchant, before anything had actually happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let the young ones take the stock list. Why not learn it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I learned software at the merchant and it still replaced me. I'd rather be good at digging than bad at a screen. That's not stubbornness, that's my experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody much. Walt's two years off retiring and the lads are young and quick. If anyone's surplus, it's me, and I know it.

S1.say: She'd say it's sensible to use what works and leave the rest, and that the co-op shouldn't buy things just because big companies do.
S1.think: Privately she thinks the small co-op would change last, which helps her, but that planning and stock would go onto computers first. Her paper niche would vanish and she'd be the slow digger again.
S1.do: Waits to see what the co-op actually does before acting, and saves about 50 more a month by cutting the newspaper and a streaming service. Lets younger colleagues take over the stock list if it goes digital rather than learning it.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like the period after the merchant was sold but before anything happened.
S1.quote: I'd rather be good at digging than bad at a screen.
S1.fieldNote: Priya's resistance to new tools is reasoned rather than stubborn: she learned software before and was replaced anyway. She expects her small employer to be slow, and counts on that. She calmly names herself as the most surplus person on the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a mess and that someone should have seen it coming. I wouldn't blame one party or another; they'd all be caught out. In public I'd mostly keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I don't think Highland Rural would have robots in two years. We still have a paper map of the lines on the office wall. The danger is the big companies get them, power gets cheaper, and the co-op merges with someone bigger who does to me what the chain did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop all extras straight away: no holiday, no new car, Ken's sister's birthday on a budget. I'd try to get to five months saved by the end of the year. And I'd ask the co-op office what my pension would be at 60, in case the merger letter comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicked, because I've got some time while the co-op catches up, but anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the co-op would be slow. How long do you think you'd have?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My guess is two or three years after the robots arrive, before a place like ours can afford them or gets swallowed up. I could be wrong. I'd be about 62 by then, which is close enough to the end to manage, just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ken that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd show him the notebook. I'd say here's what we've got and here's what we'd need, and we'd work out where the gap is. Ken's calm about money because I'm not.

S2.say: She'd say it was a mess that someone should have foreseen, without blaming any one party. In public she'd mostly keep her head down.
S2.think: Privately she doubts her small co-op would have robots within two years, since it still uses a paper map. Her fear is a merger with a bigger company, like the chain that took over her last employer.
S2.do: Cuts all extras at once, including holidays and a new car, and aims to reach five months of savings by year end. Asks the co-op office what her pension would be at 60 in case a merger comes.
S2.feel: Anxious but not panicked, because her slow employer gives her some time.
S2.quote: We still have a paper map of the lines on the office wall.
S2.fieldNote: Priya's estimate of her risk rests on the co-op being slow and poor, which buys her a couple of years even in the fastest picture. Her fear is a takeover, not the robots themselves. Money talk with her partner centres on her household notebook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the sensible people to plan, if they bother. I'd say it quietly, to the lads on the crew, not online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years puts it at 2031, and with the co-op's slowness it reaches me maybe 2033. I'd be 64 or 65. That's almost my retirement anyway. Honestly, it would land about when I'm hanging up the belt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep saving, putting the extra into the pension instead of the bank, because that's what pays later. I'd plan to stop at 64 if it looked like it was coming. I'd wait and see how the co-op handles it before doing anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly fine. I've done the sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've done the sums. What do they say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I stop at 64 we lose about a fifth of the pension compared with 66. That's a lot of coins, but we'd manage with Ken's bit and his state pension. We'd give up the car and keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone in your family you'd worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger son, Haru, runs a bike repair shop. I don't think robots fix bikes for people who want a chat, but I don't know. The older one's in the army, and they'll always need people, I'd have thought.

S3.say: She'd quietly tell her crew that five years gives sensible people time to plan, if they bother. She wouldn't say it online.
S3.think: Privately she expects it to reach her slow co-op around 2033, when she'd be 64 or 65 and close to retirement anyway. She sees it landing about when she'd hang up her belt.
S3.do: Keeps working and saving, putting the extra into her pension rather than the bank. Plans to stop at 64 if the change looks close and waits to see how the co-op handles it.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly fine, because she has done the sums.
S3.quote: Honestly, it would land about when I'm hanging up the belt.
S3.fieldNote: For Priya the gap between five-year and two-year AGI is all about timing against her retirement. She has already priced early retirement at 64 to the nearest fifth. Her calm comes from arithmetic, not from optimism.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's plenty of time, so people should get on with their lives and plan sensibly. I'd say that to anyone who asked, which wouldn't be many people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't touch me. I'd be retired at 66 in 2034, two years before. I'd feel for the young ones on the crew, but that's their decade to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Finish the apprenticeship, work to 66, take the full pension. I'd keep an eye on it and see how things go, but I wouldn't change a thing for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's somebody else's weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you say anything to the young ones on the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum, who's 22, to save more than he thinks he needs. That's all I know how to teach. I wouldn't tell him to learn computers, because look where it got me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years is a long time. Could anything change your mind?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the co-op merged early, yes. Then it's the merchant all over again, and the robots don't matter, the head office does. Short of that, I'm finishing my eight years.

S4.say: She'd tell anyone who asked that there's plenty of time and people should plan sensibly and get on with life.
S4.think: Privately it doesn't touch her: she'd retire at 66 in 2034, two years before it lands. She feels for the young crew members but sees it as their decade to plan.
S4.do: Carries on, finishes the apprenticeship, works to 66 and takes the full pension. Keeps an eye on events but changes nothing for now.
S4.feel: Calm, as if it were somebody else's weather.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Priya simply retires before the change, and she sees no need to act. The only thing that would shake her is an early co-op merger, which shows her real fear is ownership, not technology. Her only advice to the young is to save.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, but really because of what it might do to the co-op, not the robots on their own. What would help is the co-op staying independent and a pension that doesn't punish you for going a couple of years early. That's all. I don't want a course, I want my eight years.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked who owns the place you work. That decided everything for me last time. A chain with a head office doesn't care how good your books are. A co-op at least has to look its members in the eye at the annual meeting.

headlineQuote: A chain with a head office doesn't care how good your books are.
portrait: Priya Nakamura is a 58-year-old junior on a six-person crew at Highland Rural Electric, a small customer-owned co-op in hill country, after thirty years as a bookkeeper at a builders' merchant that was bought by a chain. She avoids new technology, never uses AI, and keeps both the crew's stock list and her household books on paper. She's pragmatic and blames no single party, but her real fear is a takeover by a bigger company, as happened before. AGI in two years makes her anxious, cushioned only by how slow the co-op would be to buy robots. With five or ten years she expects to reach retirement before it touches her, and she has priced the options to the coin.
biggestWorry: AGI in two years, mainly because it could push her small co-op into a merger with a bigger company that would treat her the way the chain did.
whatWouldHelp: The co-op staying independent and a pension that doesn't penalise her for stopping a couple of years early, not a retraining course.
